item.title: CUNY Has Raised $312 Million. The Chancellor Explains Why.
item.description:
Good morning. It’s Monday. Today we’ll find out about fund-raising for the City University of New York.

And, something new: the Monday quiz. On Mondays, we’ll ask a question about a story that we featured in New York Today the previous week. We’ll give you four possible answers. You can click on one of them and find out whether you’re right.

This week Félix Matos Rodríguez, the chancellor of the City University of New York, will use part of his annual state-of-the-university address to talk about big-money fund-raising — specifically, that CUNY took in $312 million in donations during the 2026 fiscal year, 26 percent more than in fiscal year 2025.

It was the first time that CUNY had collected more than $300 million in donations in a single year, and the money lifted the university’s total over the last four years to just under $1.1 billion.

Matos Rodríguez told me that CUNY cannot live by tax dollars alone, arguing that the university could not keep up if it did not augment the government money it receives. Of CUNY’s $4.9 billion budget, roughly $2.8 billion comes directly from the state and $833 million from the city. The rest — about $1.3 billion — comes from tuition, including students’ financial aid.

Matos Rodríguez told me that state and city funding for education in New York continued to rank among the highest in the nation, but that “the reality is our costs have increased” at the same time that “what the university does is becoming increasingly complex.”

In seeking donations, CUNY is following the pack. Colleges and universities raised $78 billion during the 2025 fiscal year, according to the Council for Advancement and Support of Education. Like CUNY, nearly two-thirds of the public institutions surveyed received more in donations in 2025 than in fiscal year 2024. In fact, the public colleges and universities had a very good year last year: In percentage terms, they led their private counterparts in donor pledges and promises to give.

That’s at least partly because they are paying more attention to fund-raising than they once did. Like many public universities, CUNY has expanded its development staff and its fund-raising infrastructure. “We got to that race later, so we have catch-up work to do,” Matos Rodríguez said.

CUNY has scored with nonprofits that see its mission as essential to the city’s future. “If you care about economic mobility for kids who grow in New York City, you have to care about CUNY,” said Cass Conrad, the executive director of the Carroll and Milton Petrie Foundation, which contributed $5.7 million in funding for CUNY in the last year. “We recognize that CUNY lifts more people into the middle class than any other institution in the city.”

Matos Rodríguez said he has been working to reach potential donors. He spent much of one day last week at the annual conference of Grantmakers for Education, a network for educational philanthropy that brings together foundation officials and donors.

He says that federal and state tuition programs cover the basics for roughly three in four CUNY students, but that money doesn’t pay for initiatives that would make CUNY students “more competitive in a job interview.” Neither does it help with emergencies for students struggling with high housing costs or food insecurity. And the equipment in classrooms and laboratories needs to be kept up-to-date, too.

It’s a story CUNY has attempted to present before, but one it is now advancing with new urgency. Twenty-five years ago, the 23 colleges and professional schools in the CUNY system together raised just over $56 million. In 2011, that figure was $201 million — and, by then, fund-raising proficiency had become a part of the 23 presidents’ annual performance reviews.

But fund-raising slipped, even as CUNY grew, adding two new schools. In 2019, when Matos Rodríguez was named chancellor, CUNY collected $161.8 million. (CUNY now counts 26 campuses; its medical school, which had been a part of City College, became its own graduate-level institution in 2024.)

Matos Rodríguez said the payoff for what he called “the storytelling” was — no surprise — a bigger bottom line, with money from donors “you cannot lobby directly to,” like the billionaire MacKenzie Scott. Last year, she gave $50 million to Lehman College in the Bronx. She had given Lehman $30 million in 2020 and has given $50 million to five other CUNY campuses in that time.

“You hope you get on her radar,” Matos Rodríguez said.

This question comes from a recent edition of New York Today. Click on the answer you think is correct. You’ll go to the full article we published. The link is free.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the leader of the City Council agreed on legislation that would ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park. What did the mayor say in a social media post?

“I’ve never liked horses myself.”

“This is one of those issues that should have been dealt with before I got here.”

“Our administration will make sure workers and owners are protected and the horses are safe.”

“Our administration also considered a profit-sharing arrangement with the 150 active and licensed carriage drivers, but we couldn’t work that out.”

Weather

Expect a sunny day with a high near 65. It will be cloudy in the evening, and the temperature will dip near 51.

ALTERNATE-SIDE PARKING

In effect until Nov. 1 (All Saints’ Day).

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“Republicans are talking about issues like crime, which concerned us, like, two or three years ago. Everyone knows it’s their party and Trump who are responsible for the economic crisis. It’s their responsibility.” — Assemblyman Charles Lavine, a Democrat on Long Island who is backing Gov. Kathy Hochul over her Republican challenger, Bruce Blakeman.

An ICE target: Oscar Belgal’s attempts to fly under the radar quickly spiraled after he arrived in the city from the Dominican Republic in 2022. On Oct. 8, while Belgal was in a parked car with his 5-year-old son, a team of ICE officers in plain clothes surprised them, bringing a sudden hail of gunfire to the Marble Hill neighborhood.

The first weekend of Cornell’s fraternity party ban: “Collegetown was a ghost town compared to previous years,” a junior at Cornell said. The school imposed the moratorium on parties at fraternity houses during the academic year as a safety measure amid the uproar over a sexual assault lawsuit filed last month by a former student known as Jane Doe.

The O.J. Simpson case: More than 30 years after his double-murder trial in Los Angeles, new information has surfaced from interviews and recently unsealed New York court records that described an informant who had talked about the supposed location of the missing murder weapon.

Inside Mira Nair’s Diwali dinner: Authors, artists, filmmakers and writers gathered at an Indian bistro near Gramercy Park to celebrate the Hindu festival of Diwali last week. One of the co-hosts was the Oscar-nominated filmmaker who is Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s mother and has become one of most recognizable matriarchs in the South Asian diaspora. (The mayor did not attend.)

METROPOLITAN diary

Dear Diary:

I was forced out of my Carroll Gardens home so a developer could tear it down. As a divorced mother, where would I find a three-bedroom for my two teens and me at an affordable rent?

I searched high and low and ended up moving south to Sunset Park. I found a raw loft space, which I fixed up. (Yes, I invested my own money in a rental.)

The apartment was directly above a 24-hour sex shop and it had a view of the Brooklyn Queens Expressway. I refused to open the windows and bought air purifiers.

Our first night there, I cried. What have I done? The noise from the B.Q.E., the constant shaking of the apartment — it all felt unbearable.

I was so depressed I wanted to leave the city altogether, but my kids were still in high school. I had no choice. I was trapped.

The next morning, I went for a long, anxious walk. I bumped into a barber who had been born and raised in the neighborhood, on Third Avenue.

I asked how he dealt with the noise and traffic.

He laughed.

“Are you kidding me?” he said. “It’s my ocean.”

The big trucks, he explained, were crashing waves; small cars, ripples; and the whirring engines, the steady flow of water. He told me he missed these sounds whenever he went to the country.

His perspective changed everything. The second night, I slept like a baby, with a sound machine accompanying the “waves” of nighttime traffic.

Two years later, my home is a haven for my kids and me, and I fall asleep each night to the soothing rhythm of a Brooklyn “ocean.”

— Mara Stephens

Illustrated by Agnes Lee. Tell us your New York story here and read more Metropolitan Diary here.

Glad we could get together here. See you tomorrow. — J.B.

Davaughnia Wilson and Ed Shanahan contributed to New York Today. You can reach the team at nytoday@nytimes.com.

item.title: A Social Media Mob
item.description:
Good morning. It’s so nice to be back. There’s a lot for us to catch up on, but first, I want to talk about a growing online movement.

After a former Cornell University student named seven men in a lawsuit and accused them of sexual assault, a movement gained steam online to reveal her identity.

One post offered $5,000 for the name and photos of Jane Doe. Within a day, commenters were circulating a woman’s name and photos of her from a social media account.

An analysis found more than 11,000 accounts that had made almost 25,000 posts that purported to name her. Many of those posts included hateful or antagonistic language, and some used misspelled words such as “sIut” instead of “slut,” in apparent attempts to evade the platforms’ text filters. Read the full story here.

We’re also covering:

Riots in France

A campus influencer

The Elizabeth Holmes documentary

What you need to know to be the smartest person in class today.

1. There were huge riots in France this weekend. Anti-government demonstrations devolved into riots and looting that led to nearly 2,400 arrests on Saturday and widespread damage. Read more about the protests.

2. President Trump endorsed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the upcoming Israeli election. Trump praised Netanyahu on social media, saying that any other choice would be the “wrong Leader.” Israelis are heading to the polls next week.

3. Trump said he was making progress on a peace deal with Russia. He defended his decision to ease tariffs and other sanctions against Russia. He also hinted at a hostage deal, but did not specify whose release he was seeking.

4. New findings challenge the narrative around the O.J. Simpson case. Newly unsealed records and interviews show that an “extremely reliable” informant told the authorities about the missing murder weapon. Read the investigation and takeaways.

5. Who are ICE officers really targeting? The Department of Homeland Security has said that it’s pursuing “the worst of the worst” criminals, but data shows that arrests of people with no criminal records have soared. Watch the video.

What you’re wearing.

Zinia Lee, 20, is a fashion production management major at the Fashion Institute of Technology. She’s also a content creator with more than 100,000 followers on Instagram. I asked her a few questions:

Tell me about this outfit. I love wearing pink, so I started with the polka-dot dress and felt it needed a little more pizazz, so I added the lace shrug to spice it up and add a whimsy factor. The Gentle Monster glasses I use to see the board at school have silver and pink gems, so I matched them with long, dangly earrings that feature silver and pink gemstones. I adore a matching moment, like the black boots and black polka dots or even my pink hair to my pink dress and bag! The goal is always to look like Draculaura from “Monster High.”

Who are your other style inspirations? Lisa from Blackpink. Alexandra Leclerc. The main character of “It’s Okay to Not Be Okay.”

Have you been recognized on campus? Yes! (One student told her that she’s one of the reasons she came to FIT.)

Who is your favorite on-campus influencer? Tell me here. And send me your Fit Checks!

Miami is at the top of The Associated Press’s college football poll for the first time since 2002 after the team beat its rival Florida State. Read more about the game, and take a look at all the college football winners and losers from Week 7.

The student paper at the University of Florida is celebrating its 120th anniversary today. “Some of the challenges we face today might sound surreal to those first editors, who lived in a 45-state U.S. and wouldn’t see widespread modern air-conditioning until nearly half a century later,” The Alligator’s editorial board writes.

Forty-eight students from New York University, Pratt Institute, the University of Pennsylvania, Savannah College of Art and Design and more shared their fit checks, advice and music with The Fader. These students have better music taste than me …

The stories about to hit your group chat.

It’s a big moment for Zara Larsson. She has long dreamed of being a pop star. This year, she unlocked pop superstardom. (As a fan, I couldn’t be happier.) Watch her interview on “Popcast.”

The Elizabeth Holmes documentary is out. And I’m dying to watch it. The nearly three-hour film, “You Can See Everything,” opened to more than 2,000 sold-out shows after being released on 855 screens. Does it live up to the hype? Tell me!

Do this to get ahead.

Make some comfort food. For me, the most nourishing meals always include rice. Try one of these recipes.

Don’t lose your temper. I know, it’s easier said than done. Keep your anger in check with these three tools.

How does The New York Times make tough calls? If you’re curious, you should subscribe to our new newsletter, The Backstory. Subscribe here.

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. This newsletter is powered by your submissions — tell us about your classes, questions, crushes, side hustles and obsessions here.

Also: Times access is free for half of all U.S. college students through their school. Tell your friends to check if their school provides free access.

And forward this to your roommate, professor, club president or T.A. See you tomorrow!

Want more of today’s top stories? Tune in to “The Headlines,” our podcast that includes top headlines and analysis.

Any tips or feedback? I’m all ears. Email me at extracredit@nytimes.com

The editor of Extra Credit is Talya Minsberg. Brent Lewis was our photo editor.

item.title: The French Fantasy Is Coming to an End
item.description:
On Saturday, protests shut down large swaths of Paris. In parts of the city and around the country, pockets of these demonstrations turned violent. Looting and arson marked streets near Place de la République and in the First Arrondissement, where shop windows were broken and electric bikes were set on fire. In the city of Limoges, the 19th-century Hôtel de Ville went up in flames; in Lyon, a tourist office blazed.

Protests here began in late September with students in the suburbs exhausted by the conditions of their schools, including their inability to cool or heat classrooms, keep out rats or simply keep teachers. This weekend, hundreds of thousands of French men and women joined the students on the streets in an expression of mass frustration over the cost of living, extreme wealth disparity, government paralysis and a faltering social welfare system.

For the past decade, I have spent part of every year in Paris. Protests are a fact of life here, but Saturday’s were different, larger, more intense. Many groups, including the Gilets Jaunes (Yellow Vests) — a protest movement that seized the country in 2018 and 2019 over the falling quality of life — joined the students, along with labor unions.

I left the Left Bank and set out on foot for the Bastille, 30 minutes away across the Seine, on Saturday around noon. The Bastille column was covered in graffiti from a demonstration the previous week. There I caught the tail end of a procession of people making their way toward Place de la République. It was a largely peaceful group of mostly young people, some holding signs mocking President Emmanuel Macron, some waving French flags. Intermittently, marchers would break out in chanting and clapping.

At République, police officers ringed the square, dressed in riot gear as though preparing to go to war. It was crowded but civil. Some people wore surgical masks, others gas masks, ready for tear gas, the faint smell of which was already in the air. Television crews interviewed protesters. A few climbed the statue of Marianne, the symbol of the French Republic, and waved French flags. Shortly after I arrived, flash bangs began going off on one of the side streets toward Canal St. Martin, and canisters of tear gas could be seen sailing through the air. Crowds began running back into the square. As the tear gas grew thicker, I sought a quick exit down the narrow path the police had provided for people to leave.

It was only on Sunday that I saw the shattered windows, looted stores and charred remains of electric bikes.

The violence of the protests, which was amplified on social media and apparently the result of rioters exploiting the moment, threatens to undermine the message of the students and risks resulting in the exact opposite of their goals, which is to petition for more government resources devoted to education and, by extension, a more sustainable future.

These days of protest and rage have struck me as more than just a rebuff to the French government. The students’ fury is giving voice to some larger social failures many of us, in France and elsewhere, often fail to face directly: the climate catastrophe, the terror of artificial intelligence, the faltering economic picture. The students’ determination to voice their anger and frustration over the future is a necessary and courageous reminder that we all need to be facing facts and acting on them.

On my bike ride home from République on Saturday, I encountered an impromptu gathering of students singing “La Marseillaise,” the French national anthem. As they passed the intersection, some set down bikes and other objects to block cars and make the trip more difficult for everyone. That’s as it should be, I thought, as I navigated past the makeshift barricades. Against the backdrop of so many destructive forces, none of us, anywhere, should be allowed to proceed easily.

Since late spring, a series of calamities, in quick succession, have taken a battering ram to the fantasy that Paris is some sort of respite from the problems plaguing the world. A number of punishing, record-breaking heat waves roiled the country, beginning in May. Temperatures in Paris soared above 100 degrees Fahrenheit again and again this summer. Joyful images of young Parisians leaping into the Canal St. Martin and the Seine were sobered by a national death toll of nearly 8,000 and fires that burned tens of thousands of acres. The spectacle of haute couture shows held in the extreme heat felt especially grotesque. Walking through the city this fall, I still see the tattered remains of silver foil hacked together to keep out the heat fluttering from windows. Every piece of store-bought chocolate I’ve purchased since summer is white from having melted and resolidified. As October began, I wandered into the Pride parade rescheduled after the extreme heat made it untenable.

And then the streets were aflame.

All this is happening against the impending presidential election next spring, which currently favors the far-right candidate Marine Le Pen. To paraphrase F. Scott Fitzgerald, chronicler of the interwar period (another era known for its wild abandon), a restlessness approaches hysteria, with menacing undertones that have finally burst to the fore with the protests. Mr. Macron, the target of much of the students’ anger and derision, didn’t help matters much by spending his Friday night with Celine Dion, dancing at the city’s most coveted concert just before parts of Paris burned.

In a speech broadcast live Sunday night, Mr. Macron made a point to differentiate between the protesters’ “legitimate demands” and “those who destroyed, smashed and looted.” He said, “We all feel anger and shame.”

Americans, in particular, have always been susceptible to the country’s siren call. Last year, France had a 14 percent increase in first-time residency permits issued to Americans. As life and politics in the United States have grown ever harsher and more punishing, Americans have craved France’s monthlong vacations and universal health care (if not the tax burden that supports them).

But now, with Saturday’s enormous — and enormously destructive — protests, the dream that there is a place of escape may be nearing an end. With their anger and determination to tap into France’s long history of revolution, students are showing the rest of the world that the only way to march into the dark future is together.

Loudly. And with cleareyed resolve. Their challenge now is to keep the violence at bay. If there is a French fantasy to pursue in these tumultuous times, this must be the one.

Glynnis MacNicol is a contributing Opinion writer. She is the author of “I’m Mostly Here to Enjoy Myself.”

item.title: The Local: From ICE watch to school closure fights
item.description:
Like many Twin Cities residents, I spent much of yesterday pumping my brakes as I drove south along a jammed Interstate 35. It was the price my family and I paid for heading north during M.E.A. weekend, when most public schools are closed for two days for a teachers’ conference.

The travel crush of the unofficial holiday weekend is just one example of how our school systems set the rhythms of our lives. Today, Shadi writes about how Minneapolis parents used networks they honed during Operation Metro Surge to fight plans to close some school campuses.

First, here are a few of today’s top local headlines:

Dylan Alverson, owner of Modern Times, announced that the South Minneapolis restaurant would close at the end of the year. The restaurant drew national attention when it dropped prices from its menu for several months in response to the ICE surge. The Minnesota Star Tribune talks to one of its most loyal customers.

The U.S. Department of Justice is suing St. Paul over an ordinance requiring all law enforcement officers to keep their faces visible and to wear identification, KSTP reports. Rebecca Noecker, the president of the St. Paul City Council, has said the ordinance was specifically written to stand up to a potential legal challenge.

Maplewood, a St. Paul suburb where 20 percent of residents are Hmong, could elect its first Hmong mayor. Sahan Journal profiles Chonburi Lee, a City Council member who led the mayoral primary in August by 13 points.

Sign up here to get this newsletter delivered to your inbox or share this link with a friend who might like to join us.

By Shadi Bushra

Parents at Kenny Elementary School had been organizing for weeks when the news came on Tuesday: Minneapolis Public Schools voted unanimously to shelve a plan to merge or close a number of its schools, including Kenny.

The parents celebrated the decision. Today, I look at why many Kenny parents cared so much about their school, and how they organized to save it from closure.

Kenny, a school of excellence

When Gloria Muñoz moved from Florida to Minneapolis last year, she was drawn by the range of public school options in the city.

She decided to send her daughter to Kenny Elementary, which had some of the best academic outcomes in the state. Other families had made similar decisions, moving to Southwest Minneapolis to be within walking distance of the school and joining a close-knit group of parents and students.

After the ICE surge

That group of parents became even closer during Operation Metro Surge. Parents used Signal, WhatsApp and Facebook groups to coordinate food distribution and ICE watches. But after, the groups went dormant, said Morgan Riehl, a parent at Kenny.

Five days into the school year, the district introduced its transformation plan, proposing to close at least 14 schools, including Kenny. The district said over email that planned mergers were determined by building capacity, transportation routes and other factors, not performance.

Kenny’s parents turned back to their chat groups, some with hundreds of parents on them.

“It was just re-engaging the same muscles we used during the winter, just on a different topic,” Seth Snyder, a parent and former college administrator, said.

Some of the Signal groups align with specific skills. For example, Alex Steinman, a public relations professional, coached fellow parents on speaking to the media. Kelly Cooney focused on teacher support. Snyder and other stat-savvy parents fact-checked the district’s data and assumptions. Rob Thesing designed the website StopTheTransformation.com. Riehl hosted sign-making parties for kids.

“I bought a button maker more or less out of spite,” Joe Filipas said.

The effort succeeded: M.P.S. ultimately paused the transformation plan.

The district still faces problems that beset other public schools across the country, such as falling enrollment and underutilized buildings, and the district has said it will need to address disparities in the schools.

But for now, the Kenny parents are rejoicing.

“I cried when I saw the school board meeting,” Steinman said.

Follow us on WhatsApp for more from parents on the M.P.S. transformation plan.

Top Times stories, selected for Minnesota readers. We have made these links free for readers of The Local.

Who’s winning the race for Congress? With midterm elections just over two weeks away, Republicans face a sour national environment. But that does not mean that Democrats, including Peggy Flanagan, are breathing easily.

Organizers of “No Kings” demonstrations urged people to vote early at rallies this weekend. In Minneapolis, many protesters responded to the search of Representative Ilhan Omar’s residence with signs that said “Stand with Ilhan.” “I was motivated to tell our Somali immigrants and citizens that they belong here,” said Kathryn Klibanoff, a protester.

Cereal is in trouble. Can a health pitch save it? General Mills sure hopes so. Boxes of Frosted Mini-Wheats now carry a banner promising “high fiber to support digestive wellness.”

Kirill Kaprizov scored his N.H.L.-leading 10th goal on Sunday night as the Minnesota Wild defeated the Columbus Blue Jackets, 2-1.

Kaprizov became the fastest Wild player ever to reach double digits in a season. (Look, we celebrate every win around here.)

What’s especially impressive is the fact that the Wild is playing this well despite a depleted lineup, Michael Russo writes in The Athletic.

Also: Mark Dowdle has kept running since Big’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship began Saturday morning. Dowdle, a St. Paulite, and 12 of the 15 starting American runners are still going, with more than 212 miles under their belts. There are 20 nations still competing out of the 67 countries that started the race over the weekend. As the global race enters its third day, Dowdle’s record suggests he isn’t slowing down anytime soon.

We’ll see mostly clear skies today and tomorrow, and the weather will be warmer than the last few days. Highs will reach the mid-60s, though mornings and nights will drop into the 40s.

One of my family’s weekend road trip stops was Duluth’s Lake Superior Zoo, which has fully embraced the Halloween season. The Primate Conservation Center features a “Lord of the Rings” homage, including this statue that is never late, nor early.

Thanks for taking a break with us this afternoon!

Sign up here if you don’t already get this newsletter delivered to your inbox.

Are you on WhatsApp? Join us there, too, to keep up with us between sends.

Feedback? Questions? We’d love to hear from you: thelocalTC@nytimes.com

Shadi Bushra contributed reporting.

item.title: Mamdani to Expand 2-K Program on Staten Island and in the Bronx
item.description:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani plans to announce on Monday that New York City will expand free child care for 2-year-olds to Staten Island and across the Bronx as the city moves to add 10,000 seats next school year.

The 2-K program started this school year with 2,000 seats in four largely working class areas of the city. A major expansion could test the managerial competence of Mr. Mamdani’s administration, which has struggled to address payment delays for child care providers.

Mr. Mamdani will visit a trampoline park in the Bronx with Gov. Kathy Hochul to highlight the neighborhoods where the new seats will be offered. More than half of the city’s 32 school districts are represented in the expansion, which includes all of Staten Island and the Bronx.

“From Co-op City in the Bronx to Staten Island’s South Shore, we’re bringing 2-K to every borough and making New York City more affordable for working people,” Mr. Mamdani said in a statement.

Wealthier neighborhoods in Manhattan and Brooklyn will not add 2-K seats next year. Mr. Mamdani has said that every 2-year-old in the city will have a spot by 2029.

Ms. Hochul has said that the state will pay for the first two years of the program. But it is not clear how the city will pay for future years when the program could eventually cost $9 billion annually. Mr. Mamdani wants to raise personal income taxes on millionaires to pay for the program; Ms. Hochul has resisted the idea.

Ahead of the first day of school this year, many early childhood centers were alarmed that they had not received funding. The administration rushed to register contracts, extend loans and deliver basic school supplies.

Beyond the 2-K program, child care providers have also raised concerns that more than 25,000 low-income families have been stuck on wait lists to receive vouchers to help pay for child care. Mr. Mamdani recently announced that officials would move more than 10,000 children off the wait list.

Many families were excited to receive 2-K offers that would help them save more than $20,000 per year on child care. Other families were disappointed that they did not receive offers or declined them over concerns about quality or convenience.

Since the city began offering free preschool for 4-year-olds and then 3-year-olds, officials have tried to place the right number of seats in neighborhoods to match the demand. But that forecasting can be challenging. Some families prefer a preschool near work, while others are skeptical of enrolling in a city-run program at all.

The 2-K expansion mirrors the phased rollout of the 3-K program, which added additional school districts each year until it covered the entire city. That approach — rather than targeting smaller neighborhoods citywide with high economic hardship or high demand — helped create a surplus of vacant seats in some areas.

The neighborhoods targeted to receive 2-K seats next year have had mixed demand for 3-K and pre-K seats, according to a new report by the city’s Independent Budget Office. In a swath of the Bronx and Staten Island, demand for 3-K spots exceeded the supply during the 2024-25 school year, the report found. Yet there were unfilled pre-K seats that year in large areas of those boroughs.

The additional 10,000 seats could be filled regardless of local demand because some parents are willing to travel longer distances for a free spot. But when the program eventually expands citywide, some of the initial seats could be left empty if parents opt for more convenient sites.

The success of the 2-K expansion could depend on whether the city can sign up new child care providers. The pre-K and 3-K programs relied heavily on public schools and early childhood centers. The 2-K system is using centers and home day cares, which are popular in working-class communities.

Child care providers have long complained about inadequate funding and payment delays. Mr. Mamdani has said that the city would hire 200 workers to stabilize the system.

Lori Cangiolose, the owner of the Playgroup Experience, an early childhood center on Staten Island, said that she will have no choice but to join the city-funded 2-K program. If she opted out, she said, parents would most likely leave for free care elsewhere.

Playgroup currently has 12 students enrolled in a private 2-K program paid for by parents, a vital revenue stream that has helped keep the center afloat when city reimbursements for its 3-K and pre-K programs have been late. But Ms. Cangiolose said she would lose that cushion if her business were almost entirely dependent on the city for revenue.

“We are giving up our businesses to the city,” Ms. Cangiolose said.

Lauren Melodia, the director of economic and fiscal policy at the Center for New York City Affairs at the New School, said that as the city expands its 2-K program, it should raise pay for child care workers, who often make near the minimum wage, and make it easier for home day cares to join.

“We want to make sure there are clear pathways for family care providers to participate,” she said.
